**Gini‑coefficient (World Bank / other reputable sources)**  

| Country | Latest Gini coefficient* | Year of data | Source |
|---------|-------------------------|--------------|--------|

| Saudi Arabia | **45.9** | 2013 | World Bank, *World Development Indicators* (WDI) – “GINI index (World Bank estimate)” (latest year available) |

\*The Gini coefficient ranges from **0** (perfect equality) to **100** (perfect inequality). All values shown are the most recent ones published by the World Bank in its **World Development Indicators** database. When the World Bank has not released a newer observation, the most recent year that it reports is used (e.g., India 2011, Saudi Arabia 2013).  

### How to verify the numbers yourself
1. Go to the World Bank’s open data portal: <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI>  
2. In the search box, type the country name (e.g., “Russia”).  
3. The chart and the data table will display the latest Gini‑index value together with the year of observation.

| Country | Interpretation of the latest figure |
|---------|--------------------------------------|
| **Russia** – 37.5 (2020) | Slightly lower than the EU average, indicating moderate inequality. |
| **China** – 38.5 (2020) | Consistent with the “high‑middle” range; inequality has risen with rapid economic growth. |
| **India** – 35.7 (2011) | The most recent World Bank estimate is from 2011; other sources (e.g., Indian National Sample Survey) suggest a modest increase since then. |
| **Kazakhstan** – 30.0 (2018) | One of the lower‑inequality figures among the listed Asian economies. |
| **Saudi Arabia** – 45.9 (2013) | The highest value in this set, reflecting a more unequal income distribution; newer household‑survey data are not yet published by the World Bank. |
